extracted.intended_audience: college and university administrators, department chairs, faculty committees, and faculty involved in personnel decisions (promotion, tenure, salary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, gathering, and using evidence and procedures to evaluate college and university faculty teaching for personnel decisions (promotion, tenure, salary). Emphasizes institutional responsibilities, multiple data sources, faculty primacy in review, and fair procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional values and clarity of expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must make clear the expectations placed upon teachers and provide the conditions and support necessary for excellent teaching; institutions should declare values and communicate them so colleges/departments can set specific expectations as to teaching, research, and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies on promotion, salary, and tenure should be written and subject to periodic review with faculty playing a central part. Making clear institutional expectations is described as a 'primary institutional obligation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Written departmental expectations, criteria, and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments/colleges should put in writing expectations as to teaching, the weighting of teaching relative to other obligations, and the criteria and procedures for judging fulfillment of expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy statement should specify what information is to be gathered for all faculty, basic procedures for gathering it, and time schedules for review; it should emphasize the primacy of faculty colleague judgments at the first level of review and include first‑hand data from various sources, including students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate evaluation data — accurate factual description of teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should include an accurate factual description of what an individual does as teacher (number, level, and kinds of classes taught; numbers of students; out‑of‑class activities related to teaching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such data should be carefully considered to avoid unwarranted conclusions and to allow fair comparison of workloads and types of teaching; this helps clarify expectations and identify minimum/maximum performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate evaluation data — multiple measures of effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicious evaluation should include various measures of effectiveness: ability to shape new courses, reach different student levels, develop effective strategies, and contribute to instruction beyond the classroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather a range of evidence rather than relying on one type; recognize and weight multiple aspects of an individual's performance; systems should reflect departmental values (e.g., value placed on teaching large numbers of lower‑level students).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of course materials and teaching artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Departments should systematically gather and examine course syllabi, tests, materials, and methods employed in instruction as part of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Care should be taken that scrutiny of materials does not inhibit teachers, limit variety of effective styles, or discourage purposeful innovation. Evidence of teaching activity (publications, meeting attendance, lectures, consulting) should also be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess effectiveness by student learning (ideal but limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most valid measure is student learning (changes in student performance), but such measures are difficult to obtain, control, or compare and therefore limited in practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficulties should not rule out efforts to seek reliable evidence of student learning; where possible, seek before‑and‑after or comparable measures while recognizing the many confounding influences on student learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess effectiveness by teaching performance (observation-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching performance measures — from trained observers, faculty colleagues, and students — can be useful; research supports reliability and validity when carefully applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use carefully applied performance measures and trained observers; consider multiple observations over time to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student perceptions as a central data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Student responses are a prime source of information about classroom performance, advising, and contacts outside class and can provide insights into multiple dimensions of a teacher's efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single questionnaire suits every department; faculty should be meaningfully involved in designing student opinion instruments. Use instruments appropriate to course type; common instruments allow comparative data. Obtain reliable data across assignments and over time. Supplement course evaluations with exit interviews, alumni questionnaires, and face‑to‑face discussions. Evaluations that go only to the individual teacher contribute little to faculty review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom visitation protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleague classroom visits can provide first‑hand information but do not necessarily yield reliable data without careful design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish understanding about who visits, how many visits, what to look for, what feedback is given, and how information will be used. Careful observations over a period of time are more useful than single visits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evaluation as a contributory element
rubrics_metrics.description: Self‑evaluation can be part of assessing teaching but has obvious limitations and should not be used alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure self‑evaluations to provide more reliable data; faculty or committees can assist colleagues in producing useful self‑assessments and interpretations of other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside opinions used cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside judgments about teaching competence are difficult to secure and should be used only when outside observers have first‑hand knowledge relevant to the individual's assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visiting teams with ample time to observe, talk with students, and examine data may be useful but are expensive; do not assume scholarly reputation equates to teaching ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness and faculty primacy in review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation procedures should emphasize first‑hand evidence and faculty involvement; administrator judgment should not be the sole or determining factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty should have a primary (though not exclusive) role; formal procedures should involve faculty discussion and vote; evaluated persons should be invited to supply materials. If a chair's recommendation differs from department faculty, reasons should be communicated and opportunities to respond provided. Dean and higher‑level review should allow discussion before formal recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional commitment: policies to support evaluation and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should manifest commitment to teaching in concrete ways (e.g., require strong evidence of teaching competence for promotion; combine evaluation with development efforts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain written policies and procedures applied fairly to all; a faculty committee should monitor research on evaluation and assist in maintaining sound policies and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize broad dimensions and diversity of teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation systems should recognize the broad dimensions of teaching, be sensitive to different kinds and styles of instruction, and consider teaching's integration with scholarship and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A judicious system should distinguish superior teaching from competent and poor teaching and be useful both for personnel decisions and for developing teachers and enhancing instruction.
